query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Local nanoscale compositional fluctuations, arising from limited atomic diffusion during non-equilibrium cooling, promote heterogeneous nucleation of secondary phases from the high-temperature BCC state in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
generation.intervention: Subjecting samples to controlled cooling protocols (rapid vs. slow cooling) followed by defined isothermal thermal exposures.
generation.conditions: The hypothesis applies under non-equilibrium cooling conditions where cooling rate modulates diffusion kinetics. It is expected to apply when the alloy is processed under moderate cooling rates that permit partial local ordering, but may not hold if cooling is so rapid that no local chemical inhomogeneities develop or if prolonged high-temperature annealing fully equilibrates the composition.
generation.structural_mediator: Local nanoscale compositional fluctuations and incipient atomic ordering at interfaces between emerging secondary phases and the original BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: During cooling, insufficient diffusional homogenization allows localized regions to deviate in composition. In moderately cooled samples, these regions can act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for secondary phases (e.g., FCC or ordered intermetallics) as diffusion improves during subsequent thermal exposure. Rapid cooling largely preserves the high-temperature BCC state by preventing the formation of significant local compositional ordering.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline of a uniform high-temperature BCC structure, slowly cooled or thermally exposed samples will exhibit a higher volume fraction of secondary phases localized at regions of compositional fluctuation, while rapidly cooled samples will retain predominantly the BCC phase.
generation.baseline: The as-solidified high-temperature BCC state with minimal detectable secondary phase formation.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is expected to break down when cooling rates are extremely high (fully suppressing atomic diffusion and local ordering) or when prolonged thermal exposure at high temperatures allows complete homogenization, eliminating the driving force for heterogeneous nucleation.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative impact of local compositional fluctuations on overall phase fraction and the specific identity of the emerging secondary phases are uncertain without further calibrated in situ experiments and simulation studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy samples. One set will undergo rapid cooling from the high-temperature BCC state, while the other set will be slowly cooled and then subjected to controlled isothermal thermal exposures. In situ techniques such as high-resolution TEM, EBSD, and XRD will be employed during and after cooling to monitor phase evolution and local compositional variations. Phase-field simulations will be run in parallel to predict the spatial development of secondary phases.
measurements: XRD phase analysis to quantify the fraction of BCC versus secondary phases.
TEM/EBSD imaging to identify the presence and distribution of nanoscale secondary phases and local compositional gradients.
Atom probe tomography (APT) or STEM-EDS mapping to confirm nanoscale ordering.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the rapidly cooled and slowly cooled samples show no statistically significant difference in phase composition (i.e., both remain predominantly in a homogeneous BCC state with negligible secondary phase formation), then the hypothesis that local compositional fluctuations drive heterogeneous nucleation under moderate cooling conditions would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, the microstructural evolution and thermal behavior of a Fe32Cr33Ni29Al3Ti3 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) fabricated by selective laser melting (SLM) were systematically investigated through a combination of experimental characterization and numerical simulation. The key conclusions are as follows: (1) Microstructural Variation: EBSD analysis revealed that increasing the laser power from 160 W to 200 W resulted in a higher fraction of the BCC phase (from 15% to 30%) and smaller FCC grain sizes. The BCC phase was primarily located in the upper melt pool regions, while nearly absent at the bottom. (2) Thermal Field Simulation: A 3D transient temperature field model incorporating a double-ellipsoid heat source and temperature-dependent properties accurately captured the thermal profiles during SLM. The elliptical melt pool shape and thermal gradients predicted by the model were consistent with experimental observations. (3) Melt Pool and Phase Formation: Residence time analysis showed that the bottom regions of the melt pool experienced shorter durations in the critical 1350–1250 °C range, limiting BCC nucleation. More recently, long-term annealing experiments at intermediate temperatures revealed that different crystalline phases could precipitate out of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA fcc matrix. Moreover, finite-temperature ab initio simulation results suggest that the free energy of the hcp (hexagonal-close-packing) crystallographic lattice in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA may be lowest at room temperature, compared with that of its bcc (body-centerd-cubic) and fcc counterparts. All these results cast doubt on the high structural stability of HEA lattices, which is obviously a critical and vital problem for our understanding and applications of these newly developed metallic materials and multicomponent oxides. However, until now the predicted hcp phase of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA has not been observed in any experiments and the question of viable polymorphism remains unanswered.

prior_attempts: Prior models based on equilibrium thermodynamics or simple diffusion‐controlled phase transformation concepts have failed to account for the full spectrum of phases observed during non-equilibrium cooling and subsequent aging.

General diffusion-controlled and nucleation models could not predict the dependence on rapid cooling rates versus slow thermal exposures, thus leaving a gap in understanding the interplay between kinetics (diffusion) and local chemical ordering.
